Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
I drift off into a world of my own
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Thirty years ago, Chidi stood in the crowded concourse of a municipal transit hub when the coordinated blasts shattered the glass canopy. He watched the crowd fracture into selfish, panicked scrapping, a sudden moral violation that stripped the public square of its humanity. The violence was calculated, a deliberate dismantling of order that left him with no choice but to run. In the aftermath, the event did not fade; it sharpened into a vivid, unblinking record in his mind. Every November, the anniversary of the attack arrived with quiet precision, marking time in a way that kept the original terror fresh. When old acquaintances began discussing the attackers’ ideologies over dinner, the conversation topics acted as immediate hooks, pulling the full, detailed chaos of that morning back into his awareness without warning. Those sudden intrusions quickly carved a new routine into his life. Whenever he noticed strangers cutting in line or heard familiar voices arguing over minor grievances, the sharp spike of perceived moral violation made the outside world feel fundamentally unsafe. Rather than risk being overwhelmed by such chaotic scenes, Chidi began avoiding crowds, steering clear of shopping centers and public events entirely. The replaying film of the transit hub did not simply sit passively in his mind; it actively pushed him toward fantasy escape, a deliberate drifting into a quiet, controlled internal world where he could breathe. He found that refusing to sit through birthday gatherings or decline invitations to neighborhood celebrations kept him emotionally anchored, allowing him to avoid positive events that might stir any hope or happiness. Over the subsequent decades, the very strategies that kept him safe in the moment began to tighten the trap. By refusing positive events and retreating into fantasy escape, Chidi never gave his nervous system the chance to process the original terror, leaving the vivid memory of the concourse completely unmodified. His isolation meant that when anniversaries arrived, there was no new experience to buffer the old one, so the past simply overwrote the present. Similarly, his avoidance of crowds left him hyper-aware of every moral violation he did encounter; a single instance of people misbehaving in the library stacks would immediately signal that the world was once again unraveling. The fantasy escapes that once offered relief eventually became the only way he could mentally step away from his own work, ensuring that every conversation topic bordering on the old event would instantly reactivate the full weight of the trauma. Now in his late seventies, Chidi spends his days cataloging returns in the quiet of his local branch, a role that once suited him but now feels like a test of endurance. He carefully monitors the patrons who come near his desk, flinching when they drop books loudly or speak in raised tones, knowing those small moral violations are enough to pull the film back. His marriage has endured, but his wife notes how he has quietly withdrawn from family dinners and holiday visits, preferring the solitary drift of his own mind to the noise of shared joy. What finally brought him to a therapist’s office was not the memories themselves, but the realization that his careful avoidance had built walls around his daily life, leaving him stranded in a past that refused to stay buried. He fears that if he stops drifting away or stops avoiding the crowds, the entire concourse will return all at once, but beneath that dread is a quiet hope that he might finally learn to sit in a room without bracing for the next blast.
